01.actor: Bonyam ben Nunyam and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
01.event: A wealthy man, Bonyam ben Nunyam, sent Rabbi a gift of four kinds of extremely fine linen.
01.summary: A wealthy man named Bonyam ben Nunyam once sent Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi a gift of four special linens, so fine they could be folded to the size of a nut or a pistachio. The passage then uses the gift to explain a word.
01.missing: Any turn or outcome; the report is a single event used to gloss a word.

02.actor: A man who betrothed a woman; Rav Shimi bar Hiyya
02.event: A man betrothed a woman with a bundle of rags, and Rav Shimi bar Hiyya, sitting before Rav, examined it to see if it was worth a peruta.
02.summary: A man betrothed a woman using a bundle of rags. Rav Shimi bar Hiyya, sitting before Rav, examined the bundle to determine whether it was worth a peruta, since only then would the betrothal be valid.
02.missing: The result of the examination: whether the rags were worth a peruta and whether she was betrothed.

03.event: When Rav Nahman came to Neharde'a he ordered the earth cleared away from the alleyway doors.
03.summary: When Rav Nahman came to Neharde'a, he told people to clear away the earth that blocked the alleyway doors so they could be closed. The rest is legal analysis of why he gave this instruction.
03.missing: Whether the order was carried out and what followed; the passage turns at once to legal inference.

04.event: A man asked Rabbi Yosei whether a widow could perform halitza within three months of her husband's death.
04.turn: Rabbi Yosei refused, and when the man pressed him on what harm it would do, Rabbi Yosei answered with a verse.
04.outcome: Rabbi Yosei justified his ruling from Deuteronomy 25:7: only one eligible for levirate marriage is eligible for halitza.
04.summary: A man came to Rabbi Yosei and asked whether halitza could be done within three months of the husband's death. Rabbi Yosei said no. The man pushed back, asking what the harm would be, and Rabbi Yosei answered by citing a verse, teaching that only a woman eligible for levirate marriage may perform halitza.

05.actor: Abaye, Rav Safra and Rav Yosef
05.event: Abaye was teaching Rav Yosef's ruling when Rav Safra challenged him with two objections from mishnayot.
05.turn: Abaye answered the first objection but fell silent at the second.
05.outcome: Abaye reported the exchange to Rav Yosef, who told him the answer he should have given: members of a Paschal group are vigilant.
05.summary: Abaye sat teaching a ruling in Rav Yosef's name, and Rav Safra raised an objection from a mishna. Abaye rebutted it, but Rav Safra raised a second objection about lowering the Paschal lamb into the oven, and Abaye had no reply. When Abaye later told Rav Yosef what had happened, Rav Yosef asked why he had not answered that members of a Paschal group are vigilant.

06.actor: Levi, Ze'eiri and Rav Shimi bar Hiyya
06.event: Straw, fodder and water were brought to these three sages through human partitions on Shabbat.
06.summary: On Shabbat, straw was brought in for Levi, fodder for Ze'eiri, and water for Rav Shimi bar Hiyya, carried through partitions formed by people who did not know they were being used that way.
06.missing: Any turn or outcome; it is a terse list of precedents.

07.actor: Rava, a yavam and yevama, and Rav Sherevya
07.event: A couple who admitted they had not consummated their levirate marriage came before Rava, who ordered halitza for her.
07.turn: Rav Sherevya objected that a baraita requires both a bill of divorce and halitza.
07.outcome: Rava retracted: if the baraita is taught, it is taught.
07.summary: A yavam and yevama who both admitted they had never consummated their levirate marriage came before Rava. He told the sages to arrange halitza and settle her case. Rav Sherevya objected that a baraita requires a divorce as well as halitza, and Rava accepted the correction and withdrew his ruling.

08.event: After his interlocutor proposed that Rabbi Yohanan meant the ascents and descents of Eretz Yisrael, Rav Dimi praised him.
08.turn: Rav Dimi recognized that the questioner had grasped Rabbi Yohanan's meaning as if he had been there.
08.summary: In a legal exchange, a scholar guessed that Rabbi Yohanan's ruling referred to the hills and slopes of Eretz Yisrael. Rav Dimi, who had heard Rabbi Yohanan, praised him: it was as if he had seen the man's head among the pillars of the study hall when Rabbi Yohanan taught it.
08.missing: The exchange is mostly legal argument; the only event is the compliment.

09.event: Rav Yosef said he had never heard a certain ruling of Rav.
09.turn: Abaye reminded him that he himself had taught it to them, and recounted the occasion.
09.summary: Rav Yosef said he had never heard a certain teaching. His student Abaye told him that he himself had taught it to them, and reminded him of the exact discussion about brothers eating at their father's table, where he had quoted Rav.
09.missing: Rav Yosef's response; also the reason he had forgotten (illness) is supplied only by the translation.

10.event: A woman, mourning her husband, removed him from his grave.
10.summary: The Rabbis point to an incident in which a certain woman removed her husband from his grave, as proof that temptation can overcome a person even in mourning. The text itself only alludes to the incident.
10.missing: The story itself: the Hebrew only alludes to it; the details (the guard, the stolen body, the affair) come from the translator's gloss.

11.actor: A debtor, his creditor, and the purchaser of his land
11.event: A man owing 100 dinars sold two plots for 50 each; his creditor seized one plot and then came for the other.
11.turn: The purchaser went to the creditor with 100 dinars and offered either the one plot as full payment or the cash in exchange for giving up claims on both.
11.summary: A man who owed 100 dinars sold his two small fields to a buyer for 50 each. The creditor seized one field and then came to take the other. The buyer brought him 100 dinars and said: either take this field as worth 100, or take the money and give up your claim to both.
11.missing: The creditor's answer or the court's ruling; what follows is legal discussion.

12.actor: Rabba bar bar Hanna and an Arab
12.event: Rabba bar bar Hanna saw an Arab cut open his camel with a sword.
12.turn: The camel died so quickly it did not even stop braying.
12.outcome: The camel was dead at once.
12.summary: Rabba bar bar Hanna reported seeing an Arab slash open his camel with a sword. The camel died so fast that it never finished its bray. The Gemara cites this as evidence, and Abaye answers that the camel must have been weak.

14.event: A heretic taunted Rabban Gamliel that God had removed Himself from Israel, citing Hoshea 5:6.
14.turn: Rabban Gamliel pointed out that the verse says 'from them', meaning Israel removed itself from God.
14.outcome: Rabban Gamliel called him a fool and concluded that such a removal has no force, like a halitza done by the brothers.
14.summary: A heretic mocked Rabban Gamliel, saying the Jews are a people whose God has done halitza with them, citing a verse in Hosea. Rabban Gamliel called him a fool: the verse says 'from them', not 'to them', so it is Israel who withdrew from God. And a halitza done by the brothers to the widow means nothing, so the bond remains.

15.actor: The Israelites and the young women of Jabesh-gilead
15.event: The Israelites found four hundred virgins among the people of Jabesh-gilead, and Rav Kahana explains how they told virgins from non-virgins.
15.summary: Scripture says four hundred virgins were found at Jabesh-gilead. Rav Kahana explains that they were sat on the opening of a wine barrel: a non-virgin's breath would smell of wine and a virgin's would not.
15.missing: The passage is an exegetical explanation of a biblical event, not a narrated episode with a turn and ending.

16.event: A father told his son to climb a building and bring him chicks; the son sent away the mother bird and took the young.
16.turn: Though he was fulfilling two mitzvot promising long life, he fell on the way down.
16.outcome: He died, which Rabbi Ya'akov takes as proof that the promised reward is in the World to Come.
16.summary: A father asked his son to climb up and bring him some chicks. The son climbed up, sent away the mother bird and took the young, keeping both the mitzva of honoring his father and of sending away the mother bird, each of which promises long life. On the way down he fell and died. Rabbi Ya'akov concludes that the reward must refer to the World to Come.

17.actor: Mar Yehuda and Rav Huna bar Yehuda
17.event: Mar Yehuda visited Rav Huna bar Yehuda and saw people carrying among trees not planted in rows.
17.turn: He challenged Rav Huna for not following Avimi's ruling.
17.outcome: Rav Huna replied that he follows Rav Nahman's opinion.
17.summary: Mar Yehuda visited Rav Huna bar Yehuda's house and saw people carrying on Shabbat among trees that were not planted in rows. He asked whether Rav Huna did not follow Avimi's ruling, and Rav Huna explained that he followed Rav Nahman, who permits it.

18.actor: An Amorite and a resident of Eretz Yisrael
18.event: An Amorite asked a resident of Eretz Yisrael how much fruit they picked from a palm tree by the Jordan.
18.turn: When told sixty kor, the Amorite scoffed that they had ruined the land, since his people got 120.
18.outcome: The resident answered that he had only counted one side of the tree.
18.summary: An Amorite asked a man of Eretz Yisrael how many dates they picked from a certain palm on the Jordan's bank. The man said sixty kor. The Amorite mocked him, saying they had ruined the land already, since his people used to pick 120. The man replied that he had been talking about only one side of the tree.

19.actor: A man who betrothed a minor girl; Ravina
19.event: A man betrothed a minor girl with a bundle of vegetables in the marketplace without her father's consent.
19.outcome: Ravina ruled that a degrading betrothal raises no concern that the father approved.
19.summary: A man betrothed a minor girl in the marketplace using a bundle of vegetables, without her father's consent. Ravina ruled that even those who worry the father might have approved would not worry here, because the betrothal was done in a degrading way.
19.missing: The case ends in a legal ruling rather than in an outcome for the people involved.

20.event: A case came before Rabbi Yitzhak in Antioch, and he ruled that collecting in the debtor's absence with an oath applies only to a marriage contract.
20.summary: Rav Aha Sar HaBira reported that a case came before Rabbi Yitzhak in Antioch, and Rabbi Yitzhak ruled that a woman may collect her marriage contract in her husband's absence with an oath, but a creditor may not.
20.missing: The incident itself: who was involved and what happened is not told, only the ruling.
